full_judgment:
Mr. Syed Md. Ziaul Karim, J:- This Rule, at the instance of plaintiff respondent petitioner, calls in question the legality and propriety of judgment and order dated 10-02-2009 passed by learned Additional District Judge, first Court, Dhaka, allowing Misc. appeal no. 270 of 2007 by reversing those of dated 27-11-2006 passed by learned Assistant Judge, third Court, Dhaka rejecting Misc. Case no. 26 of 2005 under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure (Briefly as the Code)' 

 2. Materials facts are that plaintiff instituted Title Suit no. 15 of 2002 in the third Court of Assistant Judge, against defendants for declaration of title and declaration that vested property proceedings in respect of suit land is illegal, void and not binding upon him. The trial Court by the judgment and decree dated 01-06-2004 decreed the suit ex-parte. Against which Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Dhaka as defendant petitioner no 19-07-2005 filed Misc. Case no. 26 of 2005 under order IX rule 13 of the Code no the grounds that summons were shown to have been served upon them but they did not receive the same and they had no knowledge about the suit. The trial Court by the order dated 27-11-2006 rejected the Misc. Case holding that (a) defendant petitioner failed to produce any paper relating to lease of the suit land to the others, (b) Assistant Government pleader Muslem Uddin appeared in the suit and took several adjournments, (c) Summons were duly served upon them and (d) Exhibits shows the title of the plaintiff. The order was reversed in appeal by the impugned order holding that (a) summons upon the defendants were shown to have been served, (b) there was a doubt as to the appearance of defendants through Government pleader and (c) Government should be given chance to contest in suit. Hence the Rule. 

 3. The learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that defendants failed to show by evidence that summons were not served upon them. In support of his contentions he refers the case of Government of Bangladesh Vs. Sunil Kumar Kha 10 BLC(AD)-153 held: 

 "It is seen from the order of the learned Subordinate Judge that the defendant-petitioners in support of their case for setting aside the ex-parte decree totally failed to establish that summons was not served or the defendant's were prevented by sufficient cause from appearing before the Court when the case was taken up for hearing. In that state of the matter the learned Subordinate Judge was totally an error in setting aside the ex-parte decree and consequently the High Court Division has not committed any error or illegality in setting aside the erroneous order of the Court below." 

 The learned Counsel next submits that there is no scope to exercise the inherent powers to secure ends of justice. In support of his contentions he refers the case of Shamsul Islam (Md) Vs. Dhirendra Nath Paul and others 2 BLC(AD)96 held: 

 4. On the same point he refers the case of Reazul Hoque Molla V. Afizullah molla alias Shafiuddin Molla and others 10 BLD(AD) 44 held: 

 "Order setting aside ex parte decree-When High Court Division is Justified in setting aside such a decree- The Assistant Judge resorted inherent power to set aside ex part decree. This he could not do, for, while considering such a matter he has authority to determine whether the grounds for setting aside ex-parte decree as mentioned in the Rule of the Order exists or does not exist- He cannot draw up inherent power while acting under a specific provision governing disposal of the case. As to the submission that the High Court Division ought to have either remanded the case or examined the record itself for a decision relating to alleged non-service of summons, having regard to the facts noticed and observations made by the Assistant Judge, there is no necessity for further determination of the question of service of summons." 

 5. The learned Counsel lastly submits that as the Government pleader appeared in suit in time so service of summons upon defendants were rightly exhausted in view of the Rule 281 of Civil Rules and Orders. In support of his contentions he refers the case of Messrs Nabi Baksh and sons Vs. Pakistan, Secretary, Ministry of Industries, Karachi 22 DLR(WP)99 held: 

 "An Advocate when authorized by the Government to conduct case on its behalf becomes a recognised agent for purposes of appearance, act and applications under the C.P. Code. 

 6. So, trial Court rightly rejected the Misc. Case but the Court of appeal below without reversing the findings of facts arrived at by the trial Court most illegally reversed the same which is an error of law resulting in an erroneous decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 10. On going to materials on record, it transpires that the suit was decreed ex-parte on 01-06-2004. It is the definite case of non contesting defendants that from the lessee of the suit premises they for the first time came to know about such decree and summons were shown to have been served upon them. It is pertinent to point out that admittedly one Assistant Government Pleader named Muslem Uddin entered appearance on behalf of defendants without furnishing vokalatnama duly signed and executed by them. From the materials on record it shows that the concerned Assistant Government pleader could not take any step to collect the information to respond the plaint and there is no materials that result of the ex-parte decree was duly communicated to them by the learned A.G.P. In view of such facts I hold that mare appearance of the Government Pleader without furnishing Vokalatnama duly signed by the concerned authority of the Government and without their instruction it cannot be treated as 

 12. Moreover, the impugned order in its entirety is well founded in the facts and circumstances of the grounds urged and contentions advanced by the learned Counsel for the  petitioner are not the correct exposition of law and facts. However, I have gone through the decisions reported in 10 BLC(AD) 153, 2 BLC(AD) 96, 10 BLD(AD) 44, 22 DLR (WP)-99 as referred by him. I am in respectful agreement with the principles enunciate therein but the facts leading to those cases are quite distinguishable to that of the instant case. So, I am unable to accept his submissions. On the contrary the legal pleas taken by the A.A.G. prevails and appears to have a good deals of force.
